title: LiteLLM Supply Chain Breach Exposes Thousands to Credential Theft in Largest AI Attack of 2026
excerpt: Attackers compromised two versions of the popular AI gateway library on PyPI, stealing cloud credentials and deploying persistent backdoors across Kubernetes clusters in a multi-ecosystem campaign.
body:
• Threat actor TeamPCP backdoored LiteLLM versions 1.82.7 and 1.82.8 on PyPI, deploying malware that stole SSH keys, cloud credentials, and Kubernetes secrets from organizations running the AI gateway library.
  • The attack cascaded from a Trivy CI/CD compromise through five ecosystems — GitHub Actions, Docker Hub, npm, OpenVSX, and PyPI — in just five days, exploiting stolen credentials at each stage.
  • LiteLLM's 95 million monthly downloads and deep integration into AI workflows made it a high-value target, with researchers estimating over 2,100 organizations were potentially exposed.

Security researchers have detailed the full scope of what they are calling the largest AI supply chain attack of 2026: a sophisticated campaign by the threat actor group TeamPCP that compromised LiteLLM, a widely used open-source Python library that serves as a unified gateway to more than 100 large language model providers.

The attack, discovered by Endor Labs on March 24, involved two malicious versions of LiteLLM — 1.82.7 and 1.82.8 — published to the Python Package Index with credential-stealing malware absent from the project's official GitHub repository. The compromised versions were briefly available before being removed, but the library's 95 million monthly downloads meant the blast radius was enormous.

How the Attack Worked

The compromise began not with LiteLLM itself but with Trivy, a popular open-source vulnerability scanner widely used in CI/CD pipelines. On March 19, TeamPCP injected malware into Trivy's official GitHub Actions workflows and Docker images by spoofing legitimate maintainer identities and pushing impersonated commits, according to analysis by Forcepoint.

https://x.com/IntCyberDigest/status/2087581727619162296

When LiteLLM's CI/CD pipeline pulled the compromised Trivy build for routine code scanning, the malicious binary scraped the runner's memory and exfiltrated a PyPI publishing token. The attackers then used the stolen credentials to publish their own LiteLLM releases directly to PyPI.

The malicious code was hidden in a single file — proxy_server.py — where 12 lines were inserted between two unrelated legitimate code blocks during or after the wheel build process. "The GitHub source at the corresponding commit does not contain these lines — the injection was performed during or after the wheel build process," Endor Labs reported.

A Three-Stage Payload

Once triggered, the malware deployed a multi-stage infection chain. The first stage launched a credential harvester that systematically collected sensitive data including SSH keys, cloud provider credentials for AWS, GCP, and Azure, Kubernetes secrets, environment files, database configurations, and cryptocurrency wallets.

The second stage enabled lateral movement across Kubernetes clusters by deploying privileged pods on every available node — a technique that could compromise entire cloud environments. The third stage installed a persistent systemd backdoor that contacted a remote command-and-control server every 50 minutes, downloading additional payloads while disguising itself as a "System Telemetry Service."

Version 1.82.8 escalated the threat further by dropping a .pth file into Python's site-packages directory, ensuring the payload ran every time the Python interpreter started — even if LiteLLM was never explicitly imported.

"This makes 1.82.8 significantly more dangerous: any Python script, test runner, or tool invoked in an environment where litellm is installed will silently trigger the credential harvester in the background."

— Endor Labs research report

A Cascading Campaign

According to Kaspersky, the TeamPCP campaign began with a single incomplete incident response. On February 28, an autonomous bot exploited a workflow vulnerability in Trivy and stole a personal access token. Aqua Security, which maintains Trivy, remediated the surface-level damage but left residual access. Three weeks later, TeamPCP leveraged that opening and in five days crossed five supply chain ecosystems: GitHub Actions, Docker Hub, npm, OpenVSX, and PyPI.

The group also compromised Checkmarx's KICS GitHub Action and AST tool, as well as OpenVSX extensions. Endor Labs attributes the LiteLLM attack to TeamPCP with high confidence, citing identical command-and-control infrastructure, persistence mechanisms, encryption methods, and the same exfiltration archive used in earlier attacks.

Impact and What Comes Next

CloudSEK estimated that over 2,500 companies and 434,000 CI/CD pipelines were exposed across the broader campaign. Trend Micro reported that production systems running LiteLLM experienced runaway processes, CPUs pegged at 100%, and containers killed by out-of-memory errors as the malware consumed resources.

The malicious versions were available on PyPI for approximately five hours, but given LiteLLM's download volume, the code could have been executed thousands of times within the infrastructure of large enterprises. The incident was assigned the identifier CVE-2026-33634 with a near-maximum CVSS score of 9.4.

"This campaign is almost certainly not over," Endor Labs concluded. "TeamPCP has demonstrated a consistent pattern: each compromised environment yields credentials that unlock the next target. The pivot from CI/CD to production is a deliberate escalation."

Version 1.82.6 remains the last confirmed safe release. Organizations that installed LiteLLM during the exposure window are advised to rotate all credentials, audit Kubernetes clusters for unauthorized pods, and check for persistent systemd services on affected hosts.
nri_angle: Indian tech firms and startups that rely on LiteLLM for AI development workflows may need to audit their CI/CD pipelines and rotate credentials in the wake of the breach.
